newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Asia should not suffer over U.S. scandal - Powell.
newsitem.headline: Asia should not suffer over U.S. scandal - Powell.

text.p: Asian nations should not be blamed for the fund-raising woes dogging President Bill Clinton's administration, the former top U.S. military officer said on Wednesday.

Retired General Colin Powell, former head of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, also said he did not believe punitive legislation would be useful in furthering a dialogue on human rights between the United States and Indonesia.

The scandal over contributions by Indonesian, Chinese and Taiwanese nationals started with the examination of donations ahead of last year's U.S. presidential elections by people linked to Indonesia's Lippo Group run by Indonesian businesman James Riady, a long-time acquaintance of Clinton.

"I think what will happen will be that all Asian policy initiatives will be looked at very closely to make sure those initiatives are based on merit," Powell, promoting the Jakarta leg of a three-nation speaking tour, told a news conference.

"I think we have to be careful in the United States not to tar everybody with this brush. The problem is not in Indonesia, China or Taiwan, the problem is in the United States with the means by which we finance our political campaigns," he said.

"What we should do is fix the way we finance our political campaigns back home and do it in a way that does not result in Asia-bashing, or in effect putting our Asian policies as hostage to campaign financing," he added.

Powell, a Republican, said dialogue between government officials on human rights was more useful than a proposed bill by Rhode Island Democrat Patrick Kennedy to cut off U.S. aid to Indonesia as punishment for human rights abuses, including those in East Timor.
"I do not think it would be terribly useful right now to place under U.S. legislation punitive acts like the type that Mr Kennedy has suggested," Powell said.

"I think the situation can be served best by continued dialogue and discussion, by us presenting our concerns and the Indonesian government responding to those concerns without punitive legislation of the type suggested by Mr Kennedy," he said.
